title: Paris: Benjamin Schmitt Restaurant
summary:
On my final evening in Paris before heading home from my annual Champagne coverage, I met with our new critic and contributor, Kate Janecek, for dinner at Benjamin Schmitt in the 9th arrondissement. Originally from Toronto and now based in Bordeaux, Kate will be covering the Loire Valley and Chablis for JebDunnuck.com. Recommended by several of her Parisian friends for its exceptional wine list, Benjamin Schmitt felt like the perfect place to unwind after two busy weeks in Champagne.  The dining room is bright, open, and airy, and despite the warm July evening, the open windows and circulating fans made for a comfortable setting to linger over dinner. Service was polished yet relaxed throughout the evening. Kate and I shared every course, and each dish arrived individually plated for us, a thoughtful touch that reflected the restaurant’s attention to detail. The staff struck that difficult balance of always being present and available, while never once feeling intrusive or hovering over the table.  The wine program is a destination in itself, with more than 900 references spanning everything from approachable bottles to mature vintages and rare finds. On a warm summer evening, we opted for something with a bit more alpine freshness, opening with the 2023 Domaine des Ardoisières Argile Blanc from Savoie before moving to the 2022 Méo-Camuzet Chambolle-Musigny Les Charmes with the lamb. We agreed the Rhône section of the list would have to wait until a future visit with Jeb.  The tomato tart was one of my favorite dishes of the meal. Peak-season tomatoes took center stage alongside delicately smoked sardines,... Read More

title: A quick mid-summer update from the vineyards of Champagne
summary:
Like many wine regions around the world, Champagne has now moved into a sustained stretch of heat and drought conditions, with three heatwaves already this season and another likely on the way this week. Spring was cool, with some frost pressure that reduced yields, though not in a way that appears to have been detrimental to overall quality. An early harvest in mid-August had been widely expected. However, the combination of heat and a prolonged lack of rainfall has slowed things considerably, with vines effectively in survival mode and ripening stalling in many places. Veraison is in the early stages, but more slowly than expected, even over the past couple of weeks here on the ground. The vineyards themselves look in good shape. Canopies are healthy, disease pressure has been low, and while there have been a few quiet mentions of oidium, it doesn’t seem to be a major concern. There is some sunburn showing after repeated heat events, but so far it looks relatively limited and easy to manage. The main question now is berry size. Clusters are generally loose, with small berries, and rain is needed to bolster juice levels. Growers are hoping for timely rainfall to help restart ripening and allow the berries, including the smaller “hens and chicks,” to fill out. Without that, the harvest may not end up quite as early as initially expected, despite the head start to the season. With veraison still moving slowly, many growers are taking a brief pause before harvest... Read More

title: R.H. Drexel: Along the High Embankments: Deepening the Wine Culture of Santa Barbara Wine Country
summary:
“I wanted to see…a lot of my painting deal with the ocean, the sky, the horizon, and environmental policy, and why not take that into the physical realm and address the subjects literally through staring at the horizon, exposing works to the saltwater and rain, feeling the motion of a ship, dealing with sea sickness. I’m curious if they remain calm or perhaps, they turn a different direction and get a little more chaotic themselves, searching for what feels more like home.” Cole Sternberg                        the nature of breathing in salt                        A predictable Pacific chill has descended upon the Santa Maria Valley this blustery June evening as I make my way inside a large Brutalist-like concrete bunker just off East Clark Avenue, not far from California highway 101. A once-abandoned underground barrel room, this imposing structure is the new home of Presqu’ile x LAND, a visionary, sweeping artistic collaboration between the Murphy family of Santa Maria Valley and the Los Angeles Nomadic Division.  The fresh partnership signals a deepening of wine culture, not only for this sub-appellation, but for all of Santa Barbara County. The culture of a winegrowing region isn’t just about the wines born and raised there, or the wineries and vineyards that populate its landscape, for that matter, or even the often-big personalities who lead the charge in building its reputation.
